title: Senior's toolkit: running TypeScript with Node
summary: The commands you use every day to run, watch, poke at and type-check a TypeScript file.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: running TypeScript with Node
steps.body: Before frameworks and bundlers, you need to run one file, try one expression and check the types. These are the commands experienced TypeScript developers type without thinking.

toolkit.what: Run a TypeScript file directly. Node 22.18+ and 23.6+ strip the types by default; it does not check them. Only erasable syntax works: no `enum` or `namespace` with code.
flags: needed on Node 22.6 to 22.17, where stripping was still behind a flag
load environment variables from a file into `process.env`
stack traces point at your lines when you run compiled JS
toolkit.when: scripts, small tools and trying things out

toolkit.what: Run the file and restart it every time you save it or a file it imports.
flags: restart when the entry file or its imports change

toolkit.what: Evaluate one expression and print the result. The fastest way to settle an argument about how JavaScript behaves.
flags: evaluate, print nothing unless the code logs

toolkit.what: Print an array of objects as a table. `console.log` is not the only tool: pick the one that makes the data readable.
flags: print a deeply nested object in full instead of `[Object]`
write to stderr, so it stays out of piped output

toolkit.what: Create a `package.json` with defaults. Every real project starts here, so scripts and dependencies have a home.
toolkit.example: npm init -y && npm pkg set type=module

toolkit.what: Type-check the project without writing any output. Node only strips types, so this is the step that actually catches type errors.
toolkit.example: npm i -D typescript && npx tsc --init && npx tsc --noEmit
toolkit.when: before every commit, and in CI

steps.prompt: Match each command to what it does.
pairs: reruns the file on every save
prints the value of one expression
reports type errors without writing files

steps.prompt: Before you argue in review, check it. What does this print?
steps.explain: `typeof null` is the famous `"object"`; `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`; `+` with a string concatenates, but `-` converts to numbers. `node -p` answers questions like this in a second.

steps.prompt: A teammate runs `node src/report.ts` and gets this. What is the fix?
code: SyntaxError [ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX]: TypeScript enum is not supported in strip-only mode
options: Node only erases types; an `enum` produces code. Replace it with a union of string literals or an `as const` object
Run `npx tsc --noEmit` first, then `node` will accept it
steps.explain: Type stripping replaces type annotations with spaces. `enum`, `namespace` with values and parameter properties generate JavaScript, so they cannot simply be removed. Most teams use `type Status = "open" | "done"` instead (or compile with `tsc`).

steps.prompt: `node app.ts` runs fine and prints a wrong result. A function was called with a `string` where its signature says `number`. Why did nothing complain?
options: Node strips types without checking them; only `tsc` (or your editor) reports type errors
Type errors are warnings unless you pass `--strict` to `node`
The `.ts` extension is ignored, so the file ran as plain JavaScript with checks turned off
steps.explain: Running and checking are two different steps. Add `"check": "tsc --noEmit"` to your package.json scripts and run it before you push; CI should run it too.

steps.prompt: Set up type checking in a fresh folder: install TypeScript as a dev dependency, then check without writing files.
steps.explain: `-D` (`--save-dev`) records TypeScript in `devDependencies`, so everyone on the team gets the same version through the lockfile. A global install (`-g`) gives each machine a different one.

steps.prompt: Which command do you reach for?
items: Tweak a script's output and see it rerun on each save
Keep a small server restarting while you edit it
Make sure a refactor broke no types before you push
Reproduce the type error that CI reported

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Use `node -p` whenever you are unsure how JavaScript treats a value: it takes a second and ends the guessing. Keep `node --watch` running while you write a script, and run `npx tsc --noEmit` before every push, because running the code never checks its types.
